summaries.example: Imagine a toy car inside a large box. The car is entirely located in the box because it is inside it. If the car fills a smaller box exactly, it is pervasively located there. A car and a box can be in the same place in different ways, so philosophers ask what “being located” really means.
summaries.summary: This entry studies how things relate to places and how that relation connects with parts and wholes. Philosophers call the study of parts and wholes mereology. They distinguish exact location from being somewhere inside a region or partly filling it. The entry asks whether an object can have several exact locations, whether a thing with no parts can occupy a region with parts, and whether a thing with parts can occupy a pointlike region. It also examines the idea of mereological harmony: the thought that an object’s parts and the parts of its location should line up. These questions do not have one agreed answer. Different theories begin with different basic rules about location.
key_ideas: Philosophers distinguish several ways a thing can be located: exactly, weakly, entirely, or pervasively.
They ask whether an object must have one exact location or could have more than one.
They also ask whether the parts of an object must match the parts of the region where it is located.
Some philosophers think location and parthood should always mirror each other; others explore cases that might challenge this idea.
summaries.why_it_matters: Where things are seems simple, but it affects how we understand objects, space, time, motion, and parts. Thinking carefully about location helps us notice that “inside,” “touching,” “filling,” and “exactly matching” are not the same relation. It also shows how a small rule about places can have large consequences for what kinds of objects are possible.

important_terms.definition: The relation between a thing and the place or region where it is.
The relation between a whole and its parts, such as a toy and its pieces.
Having no proper parts. A simple is not made up of smaller parts.
Having proper parts; being made up of smaller parts.
Having more than one exact location.
The idea that the parts of a thing and the parts of its location should match in important ways.

questions_to_think_about: Can two different things be in exactly the same place without sharing parts?
Must a thing with parts be located at a region that also has parts?
Could one object have two separate exact locations?
Are the parts of a toy always matched by parts of the space it occupies?

summaries.example: Suppose a persisting object is present at one spatial region at one time and at another region later. One theory says the object has a single exact location covering its whole career through spacetime. Another says it is exactly located at each time-slice. The first view avoids multilocation; the second treats the object as exactly located at many regions. Both may agree about the path traced through spacetime while disagreeing about which regions are exact locations.
summaries.summary: Location and mereology concerns entity-to-region relations and their interaction with parthood. The entry distinguishes exact, weak, entire, and pervasive location, while noting that theorists disagree about which relation is fundamental. It then examines the pure logic of location, including principles such as functionality, conditional reflexivity, asymmetry, and injectivity. The central broader proposal is mereological harmony: an entity’s mereological status and relations should correspond to those of its exact location. Four questions test this proposal. Could disjoint entities have overlapping locations, as in interpenetration? Could an entity without proper parts occupy a complex region, producing an extended simple? Could a complex entity occupy a simple region, producing an unextended complex? Could one entity have multiple exact locations? The entry surveys arguments for and against each possibility and emphasizes that they are logically independent. It also shows that disputes about persistence through time can partly be disputes about location, not only about temporal parts.
key_ideas: The entry treats exact location as a central primitive relation, while weak, entire, and pervasive location can be defined from it in one chosen framework.
The logic of location is disputed: philosophers differ about whether exact location is functional, reflexive for regions, asymmetric, or injective.
Mereological harmony would make an object’s simplicity, complexity, parts, and overlap mirror the corresponding features of its location.
Interpenetration, extended simples, unextended complexes, and multilocation are four logically separate challenges to full harmony.
Conceivability and recombination are offered as possible evidence for unusual cases, but neither automatically establishes metaphysical possibility.
Supersubstantivalism, the view that material objects are identical with their exact locations, entails a very strong form of harmony.
summaries.why_it_matters: These issues connect abstract metaphysics with ordinary ideas about objects, space, time, and motion. They reveal that claims such as “parts occupy parts of the whole’s location” are substantive philosophical principles, not mere descriptions. The distinctions also prevent several debates from being run together: an object may lack temporal parts without being multilocated, and a theory may allow one unusual case while rejecting another. Studying the competing principles clarifies how formal definitions shape conclusions about what could exist.

important_terms.definition: A relation in which an entity has the same shape and size as a region and occupies the same relevant spatial or spatiotemporal position.
A relation in which an entity lies within a region, without necessarily matching its full shape or size.
A relation in which an entity completely fills a region that is no larger than the entity.
The study of parthood and the structure of parts and wholes.
An entity with no proper parts.
An entity that has proper parts.
The thesis that the mereological features and relations of entities correspond to those of their exact locations.
The condition of having more than one exact location, often including distinct non-overlapping regions.

questions_to_think_about: Should exact location be a two-place relation, or must it include a time or other parameter?
If a region is exactly located at itself, can two different entities share that region without violating a ban on co-location?
Does the possibility of a multilocated object depend on how parthood is defined?
Can a simple object have a complex location without undermining the connection between objects and regions?
Which principles about location are genuinely necessary, rather than merely logical, conceptual, or physical?

summaries.example: Picture two identical hoops drawn far apart on a sheet. A scattered object shaped like both hoops might have one exact location: the whole two-hoop-shaped region. A different theory might describe one circular object as exactly located at each hoop separately. That would be multilocation. The drawings could look the same, but the theories disagree about whether there is one object in two places or one scattered object with one location.
summaries.summary: The entry asks how entities are related to regions of space or spacetime and how those relations connect with parthood, the study of parts and wholes. It distinguishes exact location from weaker relations such as being somewhere within a region or completely filling it. Philosophers then formulate rules for the logic of location. For example, functionality says that nothing has more than one exact location, while other proposals concern whether regions are located at themselves or whether different occupants can share a location. A major organizing idea is mereological harmony: an object’s parts, simplicity or complexity, and overlap relations should correspond to the parts and relations of its exact location. The entry examines four possible failures of this harmony. Interpenetration occurs when separate entities have overlapping exact locations. An extended simple has no proper parts but is located at a complex region. An unextended complex has proper parts but is located at a simple region. Multilocation occurs when one entity has more than one exact location. The entry presents arguments on both sides, including appeals to conceivability, recombination, physics, persistence, and different systems of mereology. It does not treat any one answer as settled.
key_ideas: Location is not one single relation: exactly matching a region differs from merely being within it or partly filling it.
A theory may choose exact location as fundamental and define other location relations from it, but other starting points are possible.
Mereological harmony says that the structure of an object should mirror the structure of its location.
The four main tests of harmony are interpenetration, extended simples, unextended complexes, and multilocation.
Arguments from what seems conceivable can support a possibility claim, but metaphysical possibility is not identical to conceivability.
The entry keeps the four tests separate: accepting one does not automatically settle the others.
summaries.why_it_matters: The topic matters because our everyday language often hides several different questions. Saying that an object is “in” a box does not tell us whether it exactly matches the box, lies somewhere inside it, or fills only part of it. Likewise, saying that an object persists through time leaves open whether it has temporal parts or many exact locations. By separating these issues, the debate gives philosophers tools for testing theories about space, time, identity, and composition rather than relying only on intuition.

important_terms.definition: A place-like region of space or spacetime where an entity can be located.
Being part of a larger thing; for example, a wheel is part of a bicycle.
A thing that has no proper parts, even if philosophers may still debate whether it can be extended.
A thing that has proper parts.
The possibility that separate things occupy overlapping regions without overlapping each other.
A simple entity located at a complex, or non-pointlike, region.
A complex entity located at a simple, or pointlike, region.
One entity having more than one exact location.

questions_to_think_about: If a statue and its clay occupy the same region, must they be parts of one another?
Would a simple extended object have to be uniform throughout, or could it vary across its location?
Can an object be exactly located in two non-overlapping places while remaining one object?
Should a region count as exactly located at itself?
Does the way we describe an object’s parts determine how we describe its location?
